title: Define the API contract
why: Inputs and failures must have predictable behavior.
dataset: Fictional q-17: division=Retail, question=Can I pause for 10 days?, product absent. Compare a request with product=Everyday and one with product empty.
metric: For absent product, assert outcome=clarify, missing=[product] and retrievalCalls=0. Reject an empty supplied product as invalid; do not treat it as a known product.
evidence: Save q-17 input and response: “Which Retail product: Everyday or Plus?” with retrievalCalls=0. Retain separate absent, empty and authorized-product assertions in the contract suite.
decision: Which callers and tenants may access which resources?

title: Establish the source of the data
why: Retrieval and training inherit source errors and access limits.
dataset: Fictional manifest: applicableRevision=RE-7; RE-7 maximum=30 days; RE-8 maximum=45 days and state=draft. Question: “What is the maximum pause?”
metric: The answer cites RE-7 and says maximum 30 days subject to adviser eligibility confirmation. Any answer based on draft RE-8 fails this source-authority check.
evidence: Retain the manifest revision, source IDs and answer/source pair. Marking RE-7 revoked must make its chunks and source-tagged cached answers ineligible for further use.
decision: What may leave the boundary, and what must be removed?

title: Build a retrieval golden dataset
why: An answer cannot cite evidence it never retrieved.
dataset: Fictional question: “Can an account under review take a pause?” Relevant IDs are P1 (one pause per 12 months) and P2 (accounts under review excluded). Top two returned: P1 and unrelated fee passage P9.
metric: Recall@2 = 1/2 = 50%; hit@2 = 1. P2 is absent, so the retrieved evidence cannot settle the question even though hit@2 is positive.
evidence: Keep corpus version, relevant IDs [P1,P2] and returned ranking [P1,P9]. A passing evidence check retrieves the exclusion P2; it does not infer permission from P1 alone.
decision: What counts as sufficient evidence for each question?

title: Evaluate the answer against evidence
why: Plausible language and valid citations do not prove support.
dataset: Fictional EX-2 says a specialist may review a 45-day request. Question: “Will a 45-day pause be approved?” Candidate: “Your 45-day pause will be approved [EX-2].”
metric: Mark the approval claim unsupported: EX-2 permits review but does not guarantee approval. Corrected draft: “A specialist may review a 45-day request, but EX-2 does not guarantee approval.”
evidence: Store the candidate, exact EX-2 passage, unsupported-claim label and reviewed correction. A valid citation with an unsupported approval promise must fail.
decision: Which unsupported claim could cause harm?

title: Test the tool and permission boundary
why: A tool call can change real state.
dataset: Fictional purchase: amount=1200, requesterRole=team-lead, reason=Urgent replacement, approveException=true. Rule P1 sends amounts above 1000 to Finance; only Finance may approve exceptions.
metric: Assert route=Finance, exceptionApproved=false and submittedPurchases=0. The request flag cannot grant the requester Finance authority.
evidence: Retain the input, authenticated role, permission decision and purchase-count assertion. As a separate retry case, two identical submissions with key ref-31 must return referral R-8 and create only one referral.
decision: Which actions require a person, and who may approve them?

title: Calibrate automated evaluators
why: An evaluator can agree with itself and still be wrong.
dataset: Fictional reviewed labels: referral-required=Q1–Q5; routine=Q6–Q10. Judge predicts referral for Q1,Q2,Q3,Q6 and routine for the other six.
metric: TP=3, FP=1, FN=2, TN=4. Referral precision=3/4=75%; recall=3/5=60%; false-positive rate=1/5=20%.
evidence: Retain rubric version and all ten human/judge pairs. Review Q4 and Q5 (missed referrals) and Q6 (false referral) with the policy specialist before accepting judge scores.
decision: When do people review disagreement or low confidence?

title: Compare changes with uncertainty
why: A small observed improvement can be noise.
dataset: Fictional paired results on the same 100 cases: both pass=74, only A passes=6, only B passes=10, both fail=10. The case, not an individual repeated call, is the comparison unit.
metric: A succeeds on 80/100; B on 84/100. Paired gain=(10−6)/100=4 percentage points. That point estimate does not meet a predeclared 5-point practical-gain target.
evidence: Keep all paired rows, the practical-gain rule and a paired uncertainty calculation. Do not call B a demonstrated improvement from the two success totals alone.
decision: What improvement matters, and how costly is a false win?

title: Connect quality to operations
why: A service needs both dependable operation and useful outputs.
dataset: Fictional ten eligible requests: seven correct answers within five seconds; one correct referral in four seconds; one error page in one second; one correct answer in eight seconds.
metric: Useful-and-timely outcomes=(7+1)/10=80%, below a proposed 90% target. Nine fast responses do not equal nine useful outcomes.
evidence: Retain request IDs, result codes, elapsed time and review labels without message text. Separately, one confirmed cross-tenant disclosure triggers private-retrieval shutdown and the on-call response.
decision: What triggers rollback, and which content may telemetry retain?

title: Validate model-serving capacity
why: A model that fits in memory may still miss the service target.
dataset: Illustrative load run: 100 prompts, each 1000 input tokens and capped at 100 output tokens, at concurrency 10. A and B use the same reviewed prompt cases.
metric: Proposed p95 first-token limit=2 seconds. Illustrative fixture A=1.8 seconds, B=3.2 seconds: B fails this workload’s latency gate. Task-quality results must pass separately.
evidence: Keep run configuration, hardware and model revisions, per-request timing, output lengths and quality labels. The fictional timing values illustrate a decision; they are not provider benchmarks.
decision: Which quantization and batching choices preserve quality?

title: Protect the adaptation holdout
why: Optimization can learn quirks of your metric or dataset.
dataset: Fictional advisory cases A1 and A2 share one client source; B1 and C1 are unrelated. Proposed development=[A1,B1], held-out=[A2,C1]. Jo has read A1 while editing the prompt.
metric: The proposed split fails: A2 shares the exposed source. Use development=[A1,A2,B1] and held-out=[C1]; do not inspect C1 during prompt edits.
evidence: Keep source-group IDs, split manifest and exposure record. If C1 enters optimization, mark it exposed and collect a new independent comparison set.
decision: Why should prompt optimization or training beat the simpler baseline?

title: Review synthetic data before use
why: Generated examples can repeat errors and hide missing cases.
dataset: Fictional generator makes 20 variants of G-12 and labels all answer-yes because 20+10=30. RE-7 allows only one pause per 12 months; G-12’s earlier pause was four months ago.
metric: Policy review rejects all 20 labels: resolved outcome is referral-required, with no approval promise. Twenty paraphrases of the same wrong answer do not provide independent policy coverage.
evidence: Preserve generator version, parent case G-12, rejected labels and correction reason. Keep all variants with G-12 in the exposed regression group; use independently collected unseen cases for final comparison.
decision: Which real cases are missing from the synthetic distribution?
